title: The Pillars of the Church
english: The pillars of the Church are men such as Peter and John (Galatians 2:9), who have Christ as their foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11), and He is the one here called gold. They are marble, the men Paul called a bulwark (1 Timothy 3:15), because they are steady and unshaken, and by their shining life and sound speech they bear up and support the common body of the Church.

Moreover, to love God with all one's heart, and one's neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37–39), is to bear the common body of the Church as on pillars of marble. For whoever has been made perfect in these two commandments (Matthew 22:40) is made a pillar and bulwark of the Church. So the whole body of the Church rests on these two achievements as if on legs, while the golden foundation, the base of faith, sets in their thoughts a steadiness that does not bend or shift and stands firm in every good.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

The Greek of this section opens with 'μαρμαρίνους τεθεμελιωμένους ἐπὶ βάσεις χρυσᾶς', the end of the Song of Songs 5:15 sentence that begins in the previous section; it is translated there, and the English here begins with the next sentence.
The last sentence runs across the section break: its final words 'λογισμοῖς ἐμποιοῦντος' stand at the head of the next section in the Greek. They are translated here so the sentence is whole.
'οἳ θεμέλιον τὸν Χριστὸν χρυσὸν λεχθέντα' is elliptical (no verb); rendered 'who have Christ as their foundation, and He is the one here called gold'.

'οὕσπερ εἶπε Παῦλος ἑδραίωμα': Paul calls the Church 'pillar and bulwark of the truth' (1 Timothy 3:15); Cyril applies the word to the apostles themselves. 'Bulwark' is used rather than the older 'ground'.
'καθάπερ κνήμαις τισίν' is rendered 'as if on legs'; λόγος ὑγιαίνων is 'sound speech' (compare Titus 2:8).
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u03 open
